claims.text: The initial material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 with a uniform nanostructure.
The proposed intervention is addition of 2–3 wt% Hf to W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Adding 2–3 wt% Hf will produce fine Hf-enriched nanoclusters.
The Hf-enriched nanoclusters will segregate to grain boundaries.
The Hf-enriched nanoclusters will form at or segregate to dislocation sites.
Hf will preferentially segregate at potential Cr-V precipitate nucleation sites.
Hf will form transient associations with Cr and V.
Hf-Cr/V associations will reduce the availability of sites for Cr-V clustering and precipitate growth during irradiation.
Competitive Hf segregation will suppress Cr-V-rich precipitate formation at 8 dpa.
The Hf addition will retain the nanocrystalline structure.
Retention of the nanocrystalline structure will ensure low irradiation-induced hardening and high radiation resistance.
At 8 dpa, the Hf-doped alloy will have a significantly lower volume fraction, or complete absence, of Cr-V-rich precipitates relative to undoped W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The Hf-doped alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced hardening than the undoped alloy.
The Hf-doped alloy will preserve or improve fracture toughness relative to the undoped alloy.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 forms substantial Cr-V-rich precipitates at 8 dpa.
Cr-V-rich precipitation in unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 at 8 dpa is accompanied by increased hardness and brittleness.
The proposed effect is expected to apply up to 8 dpa at specimen temperatures of 400–600 °C.
Outside 0–8 dpa or 400–600 °C, additional mechanisms may dominate and alter the effect of Hf.

contradictions.description: The baseline says irradiation of nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 is accompanied by increased hardness and brittleness, while the mechanism broadly says retention of the nanocrystalline structure ensures low irradiation-induced hardening. The distinction between absolute low hardening and an increase relative to the pre-irradiated state is not resolved.
